slides.heading: Work, Energy and Simple Machines
slides.body_md: Part 1: when a force does work, how much energy a moving body has, and how work changes energy.

rows: A farmer drags a sack along a lane
yes, the force moves the sack
A student holds a bucket still at the well
A porter walks on a level platform carrying a trunk on his head
no, the lift is at right angles to the motion
A girl climbs a flight of steps

visual.alt: Table of four everyday situations and whether work is done in the science sense

slides.narration: In daily life we say that a person who studies or carries a load is working hard. In science the word work has a special meaning. It needs a force and a movement. In this part we learn how to measure work, what positive and negative work mean, and how work is linked to the energy that moving and raised bodies have.

slides.heading: Work done by a force
slides.body_md:
When a force $F$ moves a body through a displacement $s$ in the **direction of the force**, the **work done** is
$$W = F \times s$$
The SI unit of work is the **joule** (J): $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N m}$, the work done when a force of 1 N moves a body by 1 m along the force. Work has only a size, no direction, so it is a **scalar**. No displacement means no work, however large the force.

visual.alt: Table of work done for different forces and displacements

slides.narration: Work is done when a force moves a body in the direction of the force. It equals the force multiplied by the displacement. Its unit is the joule, which is one newton metre. Work is a scalar, because it has only size. If there is no displacement, no work is done, even if you push very hard. Pushing a wall that does not move is tiring, but it is zero work.

slides.heading: Positive, negative and zero work
slides.body_md: If the force makes an angle $\theta$ with the displacement, the work is $W = F s \cos\theta$. We use only three angles. At $\theta = 0^\circ$, $\cos\theta = 1$ and the work is **positive**: the force helps the motion. At $90^\circ$, $\cos\theta = 0$ and the work is **zero**: the force is at right angles to the motion. At $180^\circ$, $\cos\theta = -1$ and the work is **negative**: the force opposes the motion, as friction does.

slides.heading: Worked example: work by push and by friction
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A girl pushes a loaded trolley 6.0 m along a level floor with a horizontal force of 35 N. Friction of 14 N acts on the trolley. Find (a) the work done by her push, (b) the work done by friction, (c) the net work.

**(a)** The push is along the displacement ($\theta = 0^\circ$): $W = Fs = 35 \times 6.0 = 210$ J.

**(b)** Friction opposes the motion ($\theta = 180^\circ$): $W = -fs = -14 \times 6.0 = -84$ J.

**(c)** Net work $= 210 + (-84) = 126$ J. Check: net force $= 21$ N, and $21 \times 6.0 = 126$ J.

visual.alt: Table of the work done by the push, by friction and the net work on the trolley

slides.narration: The girl pushes with thirty-five newtons for six metres, so her push does two hundred ten joules of positive work. Friction acts opposite to the motion, so it does negative work of eighty-four joules. Adding them gives a net work of one hundred twenty-six joules. We can check this by multiplying the net force, twenty-one newtons, by the distance.

slides.heading: Work from a force–displacement graph
slides.body_md: On a graph of force against displacement, the **area under the line** is the work done. For a constant force the area is a rectangle: $12 \times 4.0 = 48 $ J. When the force rises steadily from zero, as in stretching a rubber cord, the area is a triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.40 \times 12 = 2.4$ J.

slides.heading: Worked example: stretching a rubber cord
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A rubber cord is stretched 0.40 m by a force that rises steadily from 0 to 12 N. Find the work done. How much work would a constant force of 12 N do over the same 0.40 m?

**Step 1.** The graph is a triangle, so $W = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.40 \times 12 = 2.4$ J.

**Step 2.** For a constant force the graph is a rectangle: $W = 12 \times 0.40 = 4.8$ J, twice as much.

visual.alt: Table comparing the work of a steadily rising force and a constant force over 0.40 metres

slides.narration: When the cord is stretched, the force grows from zero to twelve newtons. The average force is only half of the final value, so the work is half of twelve newtons times point four metres, which is two point four joules. A constant twelve newtons over the same distance would do twice as much work, four point eight joules.

slides.heading: Energy and the joule
slides.body_md: **Energy** is the capacity to do work. It is measured in the same unit as work, the **joule**. When a body does work, it loses energy; when work is done on it, it gains energy. Energy appears in many forms and changes from one form into another.

rows: a moving bus, a flowing river
water in a hill-top tank, a raised hammer
a stretched catapult, a compressed spring
a temple bell, a tube light

visual.alt: Table of seven forms of energy with an everyday example of each

slides.narration: Energy is the capacity to do work, and it is measured in joules, just like work. A body that can do work has energy. When it does work it loses energy, and when work is done on it, it gains energy. Energy comes in many forms such as kinetic, potential, heat, sound, light, chemical and electrical, and it can change from one form to another.

slides.heading: Kinetic energy: ½mv² from the equations of motion
slides.body_md:
**Kinetic energy** is the energy a body has because it is **moving**. Let a net force $F$ act on a body of mass $m$ starting from rest and give it speed $v$ after a distance $s$. From $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$: $s = v^2/2a$. The work done is
$$W = Fs = (ma)\left(\dfrac{v^2}{2a}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$$
This work is stored as kinetic energy: **$\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$**.

nodes.label: Net force F = m a acts for a distance s
From rest: v² = 2 a s, so s = v² ÷ 2a
Work W = F s = m a × v² ÷ 2a

visual.alt: Flow showing how the equations of motion and F equals m a lead to kinetic energy equals half m v squared

slides.narration: Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving body. Start with a body at rest and apply a net force. By the second law the force is mass times acceleration, and from the third equation of motion the distance is the speed squared divided by twice the acceleration. Multiplying them, the acceleration cancels, and the work done is half the mass times the speed squared. That is the kinetic energy.

slides.heading: Kinetic energy and speed
slides.body_md: Because $\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, the kinetic energy depends on the **square** of the speed. **Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large**; doubling the mass only doubles it. This is why a fast vehicle is far more dangerous than a slow one, and why speed limits matter.

visual.alt: Graph of kinetic energy against speed for a body of mass 2 kilograms: a curve that rises ever more steeply, passing through 16 joules at 4 metres per second and 64 joules at 8 metres per second
visual.caption: Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large.

slides.narration: The graph shows kinetic energy against speed for a two kilogram body. The curve rises more and more steeply. At four metres per second the kinetic energy is sixteen joules, but at eight metres per second, double the speed, it is sixty-four joules, which is four times as much. Speed matters more than mass, because it is squared.

slides.heading: Worked example: kinetic energy of a cyclist
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A cyclist and cycle have a total mass of 70 kg. Find the kinetic energy at 6.0 m s⁻¹ and at 12 m s⁻¹.

**Step 1.** $\text{KE}_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 70 \times 6.0^2 = 1260$ J.

**Step 2.** $\text{KE}_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 70 \times 12^2 = 5040$ J.

**Step 3.** The speed doubled and the kinetic energy became $5040 / 1260 = 4$ times as large.

visual.alt: Table of the kinetic energy of a 70 kilogram cyclist at 6.0 and 12 metres per second

slides.narration: A cyclist and cycle together have a mass of seventy kilograms. At six metres per second the kinetic energy is half times seventy times thirty-six, which is one thousand two hundred sixty joules. At twelve metres per second it is five thousand forty joules. The speed doubled, but the kinetic energy became four times as large.

slides.heading: Potential energy: mgh
slides.body_md:
**Potential energy** is the energy a body has because of its **position or condition**. **Gravitational potential energy** is stored when a body is raised. To lift a body of mass $m$ at steady speed we must pull up with a force equal to its weight, $mg$. Raising it through a height $h$, the work done is
$$W = (mg) \times h = mgh$$
This work is stored: **$\text{PE} = mgh$**, measured from the chosen reference level, such as the ground.

visual.alt: Table of the gravitational potential energy of a pot, a brick and the water in a tank

slides.narration: Potential energy is stored energy. To raise a body at steady speed we pull up with a force equal to its weight, which is mass times g. Over a height h, the work done is mass times g times height. This work is stored as gravitational potential energy. The value depends on the level we choose as zero, usually the ground.

slides.heading: The work–energy theorem
slides.body_md:
**Work–energy theorem.** The **net work** done on a body equals the **change in its kinetic energy**:
$$W_\text{net} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mu^2$$
Positive net work **increases** the kinetic energy (the body speeds up). Negative net work **decreases** it (the body slows down, as when friction or brakes act). If the net work is zero, the speed does not change.

visual.alt: Table linking the sign of the net work to the change in kinetic energy and the motion

slides.narration: The work energy theorem says that the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy. If the net work is positive, the kinetic energy increases and the body speeds up. If the net work is negative, as with friction or brakes, the kinetic energy decreases and the body slows down. If the net work is zero, the speed stays the same.

slides.heading: Worked example: stopping a handcart
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A handcart of mass 80 kg moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest by a steady friction force over 2.0 m. Find the force.

**Step 1.** Initial kinetic energy $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 3.0^2 = 360$ J. Final kinetic energy $= 0$.

**Step 2.** Net work $=$ change in KE $= 0 - 360 = -360$ J. The work of friction is $-F \times 2.0$.

**Step 3.** $F \times 2.0 = 360$, so $F = 180$ N.

visual.alt: Table of the energy and force values for stopping an 80 kilogram handcart

slides.narration: The handcart has kinetic energy of three hundred sixty joules and ends at rest. By the work energy theorem, the net work done on it is minus three hundred sixty joules. This negative work is done by friction over two metres. So friction times two metres equals three hundred sixty joules, which gives a force of one hundred eighty newtons.

slides.heading: Conservation, power and simple machines
slides.body_md: Part 2: energy never disappears, how fast work is done, and how machines make jobs easier.

rows: energy changes form but the total stays the same
a device that makes work easier by changing force or direction

visual.alt: Table of four ideas of this part with a one-line statement of each

slides.narration: In this part we see that energy is never lost, it only changes from one form into another. We learn how to measure how quickly work is done, which is called power, and how to calculate the electrical energy used at home. Then we study simple machines, levers and pulleys, which let a small effort move a large load.

slides.heading: Forms and transformations of energy
slides.body_md: **Law of conservation of energy.** Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only change from one form into another. The **total** energy of an isolated system stays constant. Some energy often changes to **heat** that spreads into the surroundings, so we cannot easily use it again.

visual.alt: Table of seven devices or events and the energy change in each

slides.narration: The law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be created or destroyed. It only changes form. A falling mango turns potential energy into kinetic energy. A fan turns electrical energy into motion, and a little heat. A solar cell turns light into electricity. Burning gas turns chemical energy into heat and light. In every case the total amount of energy stays the same.

slides.heading: Mechanical energy of a falling body
slides.body_md: **Mechanical energy** is the sum of kinetic and potential energy. For a freely falling body, with air resistance ignored, the **total stays constant**: as the height falls, PE falls by exactly the amount KE rises. For the 0.40 kg mango, $\text{PE} + \text{KE} = 19.6$ J at every height. At the ground $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ for a fall from rest.

Just before it lands, all the energy is kinetic.

slides.heading: The simple pendulum
slides.body_md: A pendulum bob swinging in air shows the exchange clearly. At the **extreme positions** the bob stops for an instant: KE is zero and PE is greatest. At the **mean (lowest) position** the bob is fastest: KE is greatest and PE is least. In an ideal pendulum $\text{KE} + \text{PE}$ is the same everywhere. In real life air resistance changes a little of the energy to heat and the swings slowly die away.

visual.alt: Table of height, speed, potential energy and kinetic energy of a pendulum bob at three positions

slides.narration: Think of a pendulum bob swinging to and fro. At the two extreme ends it stops for a moment, so its kinetic energy is zero and its potential energy is greatest. As it swings down, potential energy changes to kinetic energy. At the lowest point the bob moves fastest. Then the kinetic energy changes back to potential energy as it rises on the other side.

slides.heading: A roller-coaster track
slides.body_md: On a frictionless roller-coaster that starts from rest at height $H$, the speed at any height $h$ follows from $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mg(H - h)$, so $v = \sqrt{2g(H - h)}$. The mass cancels. Here $H = 25$ m: at $h = 15$ m, $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 10} = 14.0$ m s⁻¹. The car cannot climb higher than its starting height, because it has no extra energy.

slides.narration: A roller coaster car starts from rest at the top, twenty-five metres high. At each lower point it has less potential energy and more kinetic energy, so it moves faster. At fifteen metres it moves at fourteen metres per second, and at the ground at about twenty-two metres per second. The speed does not depend on the mass. Real tracks have some friction, so the speeds are a little smaller.

slides.heading: Worked example: a slide and a thrown ball
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) A child slides down a smooth slide from a height of 2.5 m, starting from rest. Find the speed at the bottom. (b) A ball is thrown vertically upward at 14 m s⁻¹. How high does it rise? Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**(a)** $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 2.5} = \sqrt{49.0} = 7.0$ m s⁻¹.

**(b)** At the top the ball is at rest: $\tfrac{1}{2}mu^2 = mgH$, so $H = u^2 / 2g = 196 / 19.6 = 10.0$ m.

rows: m g h = ½ m v²
½ m u² = m g H

visual.alt: Table of the energy equation and answer for the slide and the thrown ball

slides.narration: For the slide, the potential energy at the top changes into kinetic energy at the bottom, so the speed is the square root of two times g times the height. That gives seven metres per second. For the ball thrown upward, the kinetic energy at the start changes completely into potential energy at the top. This gives a maximum height of ten metres. The mass cancels in both.

slides.heading: Power and units of energy
slides.body_md:
**Power** is the rate of doing work, or the work done in one second:
$$P = \dfrac{W}{t}$$
The SI unit is the **watt** (W): $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J s}^{-1}$. Larger units are the kilowatt, $1\ \text{kW} = 1000\ \text{W}$. For electricity bills we use the **kilowatt hour** (kWh), the energy used by a 1 kW device running for 1 hour: $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6\ \text{J}$.

rows: Small car engine at full power

visual.alt: Table of the approximate power of five common devices

slides.narration: Power tells us how fast work is done. It is the work divided by the time, and its unit is the watt, which is one joule per second. A kilowatt is one thousand watts. Electricity companies measure energy in kilowatt hours, also called units. One kilowatt hour is the energy used by a one kilowatt device in one hour, which is three point six million joules.

slides.heading: Worked example: power of a hand pump
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A hand pump on a farm lifts 24 kg of water through 5.0 m in 40 s. Find the power used in lifting the water. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Step 1.** Work $= mgh = 24 \times 9.8 \times 5.0 = 1176$ J.

**Step 2.** Power $= W/t = 1176 / 40 = 29.4$ W.

visual.alt: Table of the work, time and power for lifting water with a hand pump

slides.narration: To find the power, first find the work. Lifting twenty-four kilograms of water through five metres takes mass times g times height, which is one thousand one hundred seventy-six joules. This is done in forty seconds. Power is work divided by time, so the pump uses about twenty-nine point four watts for lifting the water.

slides.heading: Worked example: an electricity bill
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 1.5 kW geyser runs for 20 minutes every day for 30 days. Find the energy used in kWh and in joules, and the cost at ₹7 per kWh (an illustrative rate).

**Step 1.** Time per day $= 20/60 = 0.333$ h. Energy per day $= 1.5 \times 0.333 = 0.500$ kWh.

**Step 2.** In 30 days: $0.500 \times 30 = 15$ kWh.

**Step 3.** In joules: $15 \times 3.6 \times 10^6 = 5.4 \times 10^7$ J. Cost $= 15 \times 7 = 105$ rupees (₹105).

visual.alt: Table of the geyser energy per day, over 30 days, in joules and its cost

slides.narration: A one point five kilowatt geyser running for twenty minutes uses half a kilowatt hour each day. Over thirty days that is fifteen kilowatt hours, or fifteen units on the bill. One unit is three point six million joules, so fifteen units is fifty-four million joules. At seven rupees a unit, which is only an illustrative rate, the cost is one hundred five rupees.

slides.heading: Simple machines and mechanical advantage
slides.body_md:
A **simple machine** is a device that makes work easier by changing the **size** or the **direction** of a force. We apply an **effort** $E$ to overcome a **load** $L$. The **mechanical advantage** is
$$\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$$
It has no unit. If $\text{MA} > 1$, a small effort moves a large load, but the effort moves through a **larger distance**. A machine never gives more work than we put in.

rows: small effort lifts a big load
larger effort, but faster or longer motion

visual.alt: Table of mechanical advantage greater than, equal to and less than one with an example

slides.narration: A simple machine makes a job easier by changing the size or direction of a force. We apply an effort to move a load. The mechanical advantage is the load divided by the effort. It has no unit. A value above one means a small effort can move a big load, but the effort has to move through a larger distance. A machine can never give out more work than we put in.

slides.heading: Levers and their three classes
slides.body_md:
A **lever** is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point, the **fulcrum**. The **effort arm** and the **load arm** are the distances of the effort and the load from the fulcrum. For a lever
$$\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}} = \dfrac{\text{effort arm}}{\text{load arm}}$$
**Class I**: fulcrum between effort and load. **Class II**: load between fulcrum and effort (MA always greater than 1). **Class III**: effort between fulcrum and load (MA always less than 1).

slides.narration: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum. The mechanical advantage equals the effort arm divided by the load arm. In a class one lever the fulcrum is between the effort and the load. In a class two lever the load is in the middle, so the mechanical advantage is always more than one. In a class three lever the effort is in the middle, so it is always less than one.

slides.heading: Worked example: a crowbar
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A crowbar is used to lift a stone with a load of 900 N at a distance of 0.15 m from the fulcrum. The effort is applied 1.2 m from the fulcrum. Find the mechanical advantage and the effort needed.

**Step 1.** $\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{effort arm}}{\text{load arm}} = \dfrac{1.2}{0.15} = 8$.

**Step 2.** $\text{effort} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{MA}} = \dfrac{900}{8} = 112.5$ N.

The effort is only about one eighth of the load, so a person can lift the stone.

visual.alt: Table of the load, arms, mechanical advantage and effort for the crowbar

slides.narration: The crowbar has an effort arm of one point two metres and a load arm of fifteen hundredths of a metre. The mechanical advantage is the effort arm divided by the load arm, which is eight. So the effort is the load divided by eight, about one hundred twelve newtons. A person can lift a stone with a load of nine hundred newtons by pushing with only one eighth of that force.

slides.heading: Pulleys
slides.body_md: A **pulley** is a grooved wheel with a rope over it. A **single fixed pulley** only changes the direction of the effort: $\text{MA} = 1$. A **single movable pulley** is carried by the load and supported by two strands: $\text{MA} = 2$. In a **block and tackle**, several pulleys share one rope. For an ideal system (no friction, light pulleys) the mechanical advantage equals the **number of rope strands supporting the load**. In the picture it is 3.

slides.heading: Efficiency of a machine
slides.body_md:
In a real machine friction and the weight of moving parts waste some energy, so the work we get out is **less** than the work we put in. The **efficiency** is
$$\eta = \dfrac{\text{useful work output}}{\text{work input}} \times 100\,\%$$
The **velocity ratio** (VR) is the distance moved by the effort divided by the distance moved by the load; for a pulley system it equals the number of supporting strands. Then $\eta = \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100\,\%$. An ideal machine would have $\eta = 100\,\%$; no real machine does.

effort × distance moved by the effort

visual.alt: Table of work output, work input, velocity ratio and efficiency formulas

slides.narration: In a real machine, friction wastes some of the energy we supply, so the work we get out is less than the work we put in. The efficiency is the useful work output divided by the work input, as a percentage. For a pulley system, the velocity ratio is the number of supporting strands, and the efficiency equals the mechanical advantage divided by the velocity ratio. No real machine is one hundred percent efficient.

slides.heading: Worked example: a block and tackle
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A block and tackle with 3 supporting strands lifts a load of 270 N with an effort of 120 N. Find the MA, the VR and the efficiency.

**Step 1.** $\text{MA} = 270/120 = 2.25$. $\text{VR} = 3$.

**Step 2.** $\eta = \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100 = \dfrac{2.25}{3} \times 100 = 75\,\%$.

**Check with work.** To lift the load 0.5 m the effort moves 1.5 m. Output $= 270 \times 0.5 = 135$ J; input $= 120 \times 1.5 = 180$ J; $\eta = 135/180 = 0.75$.

slides.narration: The load is two hundred seventy newtons and the effort is one hundred twenty newtons, so the mechanical advantage is two point two five. With three strands the velocity ratio is three. The efficiency is two point two five divided by three, which is seventy-five percent. We can check this with work. The output is one hundred thirty-five joules, and the input is one hundred eighty joules.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Energy is conserved: it changes form, but the total stays the same. For free fall or a frictionless slope, KE + PE is constant.
Power $P = W/t$, unit watt; $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J.
Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort. For a lever MA = effort arm ÷ load arm; there are three classes.
Ideal pulley MA = number of strands supporting the load; fixed pulley MA = 1, movable pulley MA = 2.
Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{work output}}{\text{work input}} \times 100\,\%$ and is always below 100 % for a real machine.

visual.alt: Table summarising conservation of energy, power, lever mechanical advantage and efficiency

slides.narration: To sum up. Energy is never lost, it only changes form. For a frictionless fall, kinetic plus potential energy is constant. Power is work divided by time, and one kilowatt hour is three point six million joules. Mechanical advantage is load divided by effort. For a lever it is the effort arm divided by the load arm. Efficiency compares the useful output with the input, and it is always below one hundred percent.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: For free fall and slides, write mgh = ½mv² and cancel the mass.
Change minutes to hours for kWh, and kW to W before using P = W/t in SI units.
MA = load ÷ effort = effort arm ÷ load arm; name the class from where the fulcrum is.
For pulleys, count only the strands supporting the load.
Efficiency is a percentage and must be below 100 % for a real machine; check your answer.

For pulleys, count only the strands that support the load. And check that an efficiency is below one hundred percent.

sections.heading: 1. Work done by a force
sections.body_md:
**Work** is done when a force moves a body. For a force $F$ along the displacement $s$, $W = Fs$; in general $W = Fs\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. The unit is the **joule** (J), $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N m}$. Work is a scalar.

- $\theta = 0^\circ$: **positive** work (the force helps the motion).
- $\theta = 90^\circ$: **zero** work (for example the lift on a trunk carried along a level road).
- $\theta = 180^\circ$: **negative** work (friction or brakes).
- No displacement means no work. On a force–displacement graph the **area under the line** is the work done.

sections.heading: 2. Kinetic energy
sections.body_md:
**Energy** is the capacity to do work, measured in joules. **Kinetic energy** is the energy of a moving body. From $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$ and $F = ma$, the work done in giving a body speed $v$ is $W = Fs = ma \cdot v^2/2a = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so
$$\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$$
Doubling the speed makes the KE four times as large; doubling the mass doubles it.

key_terms.definition_md: The capacity to do work; unit joule.
The energy a body has because of its motion, ½mv².

visual.alt: Graph of kinetic energy against speed for a body of mass 2 kilograms: a curve that rises ever more steeply, passing through 16 joules at 4 metres per second and 64 joules at 8 metres per second
visual.caption: Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large.

sections.heading: 3. Potential energy and the work–energy theorem
sections.body_md:
**Gravitational potential energy** is the energy a body has because of its height. Lifting a body of mass $m$ at steady speed needs a force $mg$, so the work done in raising it by $h$ is $W = mgh$, stored as
$$\text{PE} = mgh$$
(with $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, measured from a chosen reference level).

**Work–energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy, $W_\text{net} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mu^2$. Brakes do negative work and reduce the KE to zero.

key_terms.definition_md: Stored energy due to position or condition; mgh near the Earth.
Net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy.

visual.alt: Table linking net work to the change in kinetic energy and the motion

sections.heading: 4. Conservation of energy
sections.body_md:
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it changes from one form to another. **Mechanical energy** = KE + PE. For a freely falling body, a frictionless slide, a roller-coaster or an ideal pendulum, the mechanical energy **stays constant**: as PE falls, KE rises by the same amount. From rest at height $H$, the speed at height $h$ is $v = \sqrt{2g(H - h)}$, which does not depend on the mass.

Examples of transformations: a fan (electrical to kinetic), a solar cell (light to electrical), a dam (potential to kinetic to electrical), burning gas (chemical to heat and light). In real systems some energy becomes heat.

key_terms.definition_md: Energy is neither created nor destroyed; the total stays constant.
The sum of kinetic and potential energy.

sections.heading: 5. Power and commercial unit of energy
sections.body_md:
**Power** is the rate of doing work: $P = W/t$. The SI unit is the **watt** (W), $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J s}^{-1}$; $1\ \text{kW} = 1000\ \text{W}$. The commercial unit of electrical energy is the **kilowatt hour** (kWh), also called a unit: $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J.

Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours. A 1.5 kW geyser used for 20 minutes uses $1.5 \times \tfrac{20}{60} = 0.50$ kWh.

key_terms.definition_md: Work done per unit time; unit watt.
Energy used by a 1 kW device in 1 hour, 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

rows: power in kW × time in hours

sections.heading: 6. Simple machines: levers, pulleys and efficiency
sections.body_md:
A **simple machine** changes the size or direction of a force. $\text{MA} = \text{load}/\text{effort}$ (no unit). A machine never gives more work than it receives.

- **Lever:** $\text{MA} = \text{effort arm}/\text{load arm}$. **Class I**: fulcrum in the middle (seesaw). **Class II**: load in the middle (wheelbarrow), MA > 1. **Class III**: effort in the middle (tongs), MA < 1.
- **Pulleys:** single fixed MA = 1 (changes direction only); single movable MA = 2; for an ideal block and tackle MA = number of strands supporting the load.
- **Efficiency** $\eta = \dfrac{\text{work output}}{\text{work input}} \times 100\,\%$, and $\eta = \text{MA}/\text{VR} \times 100\,\%$, where VR is the distance moved by the effort divided by that moved by the load. Real machines have $\eta < 100\,\%$.

key_terms.definition_md: The fixed point about which a lever turns.
Useful work output divided by work input, as a percentage.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Write the formula first, then substitute with units (J, W, N, m, kg, m s⁻¹); state g = 9.8 m s⁻².
- Say whether work is positive, zero or negative and why (the angle).
- Square the speed in KE; use the work–energy theorem for stopping problems.
- Free fall and frictionless slopes: mgh = ½mv², and the mass cancels.
- kWh = kW × hours; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
- MA = load ÷ effort = effort arm ÷ load arm; count only supporting strands in a pulley; efficiency stays below 100 %.

cards.front_md: When is work done in the science sense?
cards.back_md: When a force moves a body so that there is a displacement along the force.

cards.front_md: Formula and unit of work?
cards.back_md: $W = Fs\cos\theta$; the joule (J), $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N m}$.

cards.front_md: When is work positive?
cards.back_md: When the force is along the displacement, $\theta = 0^\circ$.

cards.front_md: When is work zero?
cards.back_md: When there is no displacement, or the force is at right angles to it, $\theta = 90^\circ$.

cards.front_md: When is work negative?
cards.back_md: When the force opposes the displacement, $\theta = 180^\circ$, as friction does.

cards.front_md: What does the area under a force–displacement graph give?
cards.back_md: The work done by the force.

cards.front_md: Define energy.
cards.back_md: The capacity to do work; measured in joules.

cards.front_md: Define kinetic energy.
cards.back_md: The energy a body has because of its motion.

cards.front_md: Formula for kinetic energy?
cards.back_md: $\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

cards.front_md: The speed of a body is doubled. What happens to its KE?
cards.back_md: It becomes four times as large.

cards.front_md: Define potential energy.
cards.back_md: The energy a body has because of its position or condition.

cards.front_md: Formula for gravitational potential energy?
cards.back_md: $\text{PE} = mgh$

cards.front_md: State the work–energy theorem.
cards.back_md: The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.

cards.front_md: What does negative net work do to a moving body?
cards.back_md: It decreases the kinetic energy; the body slows down.

cards.front_md: State the law of conservation of energy.
cards.back_md: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it changes from one form to another, and the total stays constant.

cards.front_md: What is mechanical energy?
cards.back_md: The sum of kinetic energy and potential energy.

cards.front_md: At what point is the KE of a swinging pendulum bob greatest?
cards.back_md: At the mean (lowest) position.

cards.front_md: Speed of a body falling from rest through height h?
cards.back_md: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, independent of the mass.

cards.front_md: Energy change in a ceiling fan?
cards.back_md: Electrical energy changes to kinetic energy (and a little heat).

cards.front_md: Define power and its SI unit.
cards.back_md: The rate of doing work, P = W/t; the watt (W), one joule per second.

cards.front_md: How many watts in 1 kW?
What is a kilowatt hour?
cards.back_md: The energy used by a 1 kW device in 1 hour; $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J.

cards.front_md: A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours. Energy used?
cards.back_md: 6 kWh.

cards.front_md: Define mechanical advantage.
cards.back_md: Load divided by effort; it has no unit.

cards.front_md: MA of a lever in terms of arms?
cards.back_md: Effort arm divided by load arm.

cards.front_md: Where is the fulcrum in a class I lever?
cards.back_md: Between the effort and the load (seesaw, scissors).

cards.front_md: Which class of lever has the load between the fulcrum and the effort?
cards.back_md: Class II (wheelbarrow, nutcracker); its MA is greater than 1.

cards.front_md: Which class of lever always has MA less than 1?
cards.back_md: Class III (tongs, fishing rod), where the effort is between the fulcrum and the load.

cards.front_md: MA of a single fixed pulley and a single movable pulley?
cards.back_md: Single fixed 1 (changes direction only); single movable 2.

cards.front_md: MA of an ideal block and tackle?
cards.back_md: Equal to the number of rope strands supporting the load.

cards.front_md: Define efficiency.
cards.back_md: Useful work output divided by work input, times $100\,\%$; also MA ÷ VR × 100 %.

cards.front_md: Can a real machine have an efficiency of 100 %?
cards.back_md: No. Friction and the weight of moving parts waste some energy, so it is always less.

questions.stem_md: A waiter carries a tray of tea horizontally across a hall at a steady speed. The work done on the tray by the upward force of his hand is:

options.text_md: positive, because he is walking
negative, because gravity pulls the tray down
zero, because the force is at right angles to the displacement
equal to the weight of the tray multiplied by the distance walked

questions.solution_md: His hand pushes the tray upward but the tray moves sideways. The angle between force and displacement is 90°, so $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ and the work is zero — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A weightlifter holds a heavy barbell motionless above his head for 5 seconds. The work he does on the barbell during these 5 seconds is:

options.text_md: equal to the weight of the barbell multiplied by 5
zero, because the barbell has no displacement
positive, because he applies a large force
negative, because the barbell is heavy

questions.solution_md: Work needs a displacement. The barbell does not move, so the work done on it is zero however large the force — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A brake block presses on the rim of a spinning bicycle wheel and slows it down. The work done by the friction force of the block on the rim is:

options.text_md: positive, because the wheel stops
zero, because the rim does not move away
positive, because friction is a contact force
negative, because the force opposes the motion of the rim

questions.solution_md: The friction force acts opposite to the motion of the rim, so the angle is 180° and the work is negative. It takes kinetic energy away from the wheel — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. The work done by the pull of the string on the stone in one full turn is:

options.text_md: positive, because the string pulls inward
negative, because the stone returns to the start
equal to the pull multiplied by the circumference of the circle
zero, because the pull is always at right angles to the motion

questions.solution_md: The string pulls towards the centre while the stone moves along the tangent. The angle is 90° at every instant, so the work is zero — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On a graph of force against displacement, a horizontal straight line at 8 N runs from 0 to 5.0 m. The work done is:
questions.solution_md: Work is the area under the graph, a rectangle of height 8 N and width 5.0 m: $8 \times 5.0 = 40$ J — option (b). (a) adds the numbers, and (d) is the area of a triangle.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Riya pushes a trolley 4 m north and Arjun pushes an identical trolley 4 m east with the same force along the motion. Their works point in different directions, so work is a vector.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Both do the same work, because work has only a size (with a sign) and no direction. It is a scalar, although it is found from two vectors, force and displacement.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The work done by friction on a sliding box is negative.

**Reason (R):** The friction force acts in the direction opposite to the displacement of the box.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: The angle between the friction force and the displacement is 180°, and $\cos 180^\circ = -1$, so the work is negative. R gives exactly this reason — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A farmer pulls a plough with a rope that makes an angle of 60° with the level ground. The pull is 400 N and the plough moves 25 m. Using $\cos 60^\circ = 0.50$, find the work done by the pull, in J.
questions.solution_md: $W = Fs\cos\theta = 400 \times 25 \times 0.50 = 5000$ J.

marking_scheme.step: Uses W = F s cos θ

questions.stem_md: A girl draws a 12 kg bucket of water up from a well 8.5 m deep at a steady speed. Taking $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, find the work she does on the bucket, in J.
questions.solution_md: At steady speed the pull equals the weight $mg$. $W = mgh = 12 \times 9.8 \times 8.5 = 999.6$ J.

questions.stem_md: A student holds a heavy water can still at arm’s length for one minute and feels tired. Has she done any work on the can in the science sense? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: No work is done on the can. Work needs a displacement of the point where the force acts, and the can does not move. She feels tired only because her muscles are using energy inside her body to keep holding the weight, which is not work done on the can.

questions.solution_md: No displacement, so no work.

marking_scheme.step: No work: the can has no displacement
Tiredness is due to muscle effort, not work on the can

questions.stem_md: A girl pushes a trolley forward along a floor against friction. Explain why her push does positive work and friction does negative work.

answer.model_answer_md: Her push acts in the same direction as the displacement, so the angle is 0° and cos 0° is 1, which makes the work positive. Friction acts opposite to the displacement, so the angle is 180° and cos 180° is −1, which makes its work negative.

questions.solution_md: Angle 0° gives positive work; angle 180° gives negative work.

marking_scheme.step: Push along the motion, angle 0°, positive work
Friction opposite to motion, angle 180°, negative work

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define work and the joule.

(b) Explain, with a named everyday example each, when the work done by a force is positive, zero and negative.

(c) A force of 50 N moves a block 3.0 m along its own direction while a friction force of 20 N acts against the motion. Find the work done by each force and the net work.

answer.model_answer_md: Work is the product of the force and the displacement along the force, $W = Fs\cos\theta$. One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves a body 1 m along the force. The work is positive when the force acts with the motion, as when a boy pushes a cart forward. It is zero when there is no displacement or the force is at right angles to the motion, as for a girl carrying a bag along a level road. It is negative when the force opposes the motion, as for friction on a sliding box. In (c) the push does $50 \times 3 = 150$ J and friction does $-20 \times 3 = -60$ J, so the net work is 90 J.

questions.solution_md: Definition; three cases with examples; +150 J, −60 J, net 90 J.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Definition of work and of the joule
(b) Positive, zero and negative work with examples
(c) +150 J, −60 J and net work 90 J

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student pulls a loaded trolley along a level table with a spring balance. The force is kept constant in each stage and read from the balance.

| Stage | Force (N) | Distance moved (m) |
|---|---|---|
| First | 6.0 | 2.0 |
| Second | 3.5 | 4.0 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) 12 J

**(b)** $W = 3.5 \times 4.0 = 14$ J.

**(c)** (i) Total work $= 12 + 14 = 26$ J. Average force $= 26 / 6.0 = 4.3$ N.

**OR** (ii) The graph is two steps: a rectangle 6.0 N high from 0 to 2.0 m, then a lower rectangle 3.5 N high from 2.0 m to 6.0 m. The total area under both rectangles is the total work done, 26 J.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $W = Fs = 6.0 \times 2.0 = 12$ J, the area of the first rectangle on a force–displacement graph — option (c).

**(b)** W = Fs = 14 J.

**(c)** (i) Total 26 J; average force 26 ÷ 6.0 ≈ 4.3 N.

(ii) Two rectangles; total area is the work.

children.stem_md: The work done by the pull in the first stage is:

questions.stem_md: While a force acts on a trolley, its kinetic energy rises from 20 J to 50 J. The net work done on the trolley is:

questions.stem_md: A 1 kg ball and a 4 kg ball have the same kinetic energy. The ratio of the speed of the 1 kg ball to the speed of the 4 kg ball is:

questions.solution_md: Net work $= \tfrac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.50 \times (36 - 4) = 8.0$ J — option (d). (a) uses $v - u$ in place of $v^2 - u^2$.

questions.stem_md: A box of mass m is raised slowly, at constant speed, through a height h. The work done by the lifting force is mgh because:

the displacement is at right angles to the weight

the kinetic energy of the box increases by mgh

questions.stem_md: A truck moving at 60 km/h takes a much longer distance to stop than the same truck at 30 km/h with the same brakes. Explain using kinetic energy.

answer.model_answer_md: Kinetic energy is one half mv², so doubling the speed from 30 to 60 km/h makes the kinetic energy four times as large. The brakes must do four times as much work, and since the braking force is the same, the stopping distance is four times as long.

questions.stem_md: Show that the gravitational potential energy of a body of mass m raised steadily through a height h is mgh.

answer.model_answer_md: To raise the body at constant speed we must pull upward with a force equal to its weight, which is mg. The displacement h is in the direction of this force. questions.stem_md: State the work–energy theorem. Use it to explain why a fast train needs a longer distance to stop than a slow train when the braking force is the same.

answer.model_answer_md: The theorem says that the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy. A train stops when the work done by the brakes removes all its kinetic energy. A faster train has more kinetic energy, so the same braking force must act over a longer distance to do the larger amount of work.

questions.solution_md: Net work equals change in KE; more KE needs more braking work, so more distance.

marking_scheme.step: Braking work equals the KE removed
More KE with the same force needs a longer distance

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define kinetic energy.

(b) A net force F gives a body of mass m, starting from rest, a speed v in a distance s. Using F = ma and v² = 2as, derive the expression for its kinetic energy.

(c) The speed of a 0.50 kg ball increases from 4.0 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹. Find the work done on the ball.

answer.model_answer_md: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because it is moving; it is measured in joules. In (b), starting from rest, the third equation of motion $v^2 = 2as$ gives $s = v^2/2a$. The work done by the net force $F = ma$ over this distance is $W = Fs = ma \times v^2/2a = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. The acceleration cancels, and the work done on the body is stored in it as kinetic energy. In (c), by the work–energy theorem, the work done on the ball equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times (10^2 - 4^2) = 21$ J. The speed rises, so the work done is positive.

questions.solution_md: Definition; derivation KE = ½mv²; change in KE = 21 J.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Derivation using v² = 2as and F = ma

(a) State the law of conservation of energy.

(c) A 2.0 kg brick falls from the top of a house 12 m above the ground. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find its speed when it is 4.0 m above the ground.

answer.model_answer_md: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only change from one form to another, and the total remains constant. In (c) the brick has fallen 8 m, so $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mg(12 - 4)$ and the mass cancels. $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 8} = \sqrt{156.8} = 12.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Power is the rate of doing work, $P = W/t$, and its SI unit is the watt, one joule per second. One kilowatt hour is $1000 \times 3600 = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J. Since all of it is used to lift the water, this work equals $mgh$, so $m = 90000 / (9.8 \times 12) = 765$ kg of water is raised each minute. In (c) the energy used in 2 hours is the power in kilowatts multiplied by the time in hours, $1.5 \times 2 = 3.0$ kWh.

answer.model_answer_md: In a class I lever the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load, as in a seesaw. In a class II lever the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort, as in a wheelbarrow. In a class III lever the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load, as in a pair of tongs.

questions.stem_md: Define the efficiency of a machine. Why is the efficiency of every real machine less than 100 %? Give two causes.

answer.model_answer_md: Efficiency is the useful work output divided by the work input, expressed as a percentage. It is less than 100 % because some of the input energy is wasted. One cause is friction between moving parts, which changes some energy into heat. Another is the weight of the moving parts, such as the lower pulley and the rope, which must also be lifted.

answer.model_answer_md: Mechanical advantage is the load divided by the effort. For a lever it equals the effort arm divided by the load arm.
